Abstract

Helium-bubble coarsening under residual stress is a critical degradation mechanism in Fe-based structural materials, yet its stress-dependent kinetics remain unquantified. Here, a chemo-elastic phase-field model coupling the Cahn–Hilliard equation with micro-elasticity is developed to investigate the Ostwald ripening of He bubbles in Fe. Residual equibiaxial compressive and tensile stresses are applied to study the kinetic evolution of bubble number density, average radius, coarsening rate, and stress-modified mobility. The results show that both higher temperature and tensile stress accelerate coarsening, producing fewer and larger bubbles, whereas compressive stress suppresses evolution kinetics by reducing the activation-volume contribution to the mobility. In the late stage, the bubble size increased with time, and the fitted coarsening-rate constant showed an Arrhenius-type temperature dependence. These findings provide a quantitative basis for predicting stress-biased He-bubble evolution and offer mechanistic guidance for the design of radiation-tolerant Fe-based alloys.

1. Introduction

Neutron irradiation in nuclear reactors causes a large number of vacancies and self-interstitials, which results in the complex evolution of defects and weakens the structural materials [1], [2]. These defect cascades produce transmutation products, one of the most adverse is helium, which, being insoluble in iron, forms nano gas bubbles [3], [4], [5], [6]. As the dose increases, helium collects at defect sinks (i.e., dislocation networks, grain boundaries, and voids) and increases the growth of vacancy clusters and later, the growth of bubbles [7], [8], [9], [10]. Bubble population leads to embrittlement, swelling, and intergranular fracture of ferritic/martensitic steels used for reactor vessels and core support components [11], [12], [13], [14]. These materials are exposed to strong thermal gradients with post-irradiation heat treatments that can alter the bubble microstructure and modes of degradation that limit long-term reliability and lifetime [15], [16], [17], [18]. Such a mechanistic understanding is necessary to estimate lifetime and to develop advanced strategies for mitigation in combined fission and fusion systems when coupled irradiation, temperature, and stress are used to drive helium bubble growth [19], [20].
Experimental studies on the evolution of helium bubbles in iron and FeCr alloys using in situ TEM, ion-implanted and post-annealed samples have consistently revealed that helium bubble evolution is highly temperature dependent [21], [22], [23]. It is observed that the bubbles are small and relatively uniform at lower temperatures, while the elevated temperatures cause faster migration, coalescence, and growth, resulting in fewer larger bubbles and more heterogeneous spatial distribution [24], [25], [26]. It has been shown through in situ heating studies that bubble number density decreases over time and the average bubble radius increases. This phenomenon is called “coarsening kinetics,” which is seen in diffusion-controlled Ostwald ripening and migration-coalescence mechanisms [27], [28], [29]. Studies have shown microstructural sinks, including grain boundaries and dislocations, to be favorable bubble nucleation and growth sites [30], [31], [32].
Recent experimental studies also show that the shape and stability of the bubbles are not only affected by external or residual stresses but also by the influence of stress on bubble kinetics, which is difficult to separate in most experiments because of the absence of separation of the thermal history, defect density, and irradiation conditions [33], [34], [35]. These challenges motivate computational studies that systematically vary temperature and stress while other variables are held constant [36], [37].
The classical theory of coarsening is known as the Ostwald ripening theory, which says that the mean bubble radius increases as (𝑟 ∝𝑡1/3) in the dilute diffusion-controlled regime [38], [39], [40]. Theories that have been extended to LSW include finite volume fractions, elastic strain energy, and interaction effects that can alter the growth exponents and alter the size distributions [41], [42], [43], [44], [45]. The phase-field method is a powerful mesoscale model for describing the above-mentioned microstructural evolution, in which interfaces are modeled as diffuse regions, topological change is readily incorporated, and multi-bubble systems can be modeled without any interface tracking [46], [47].
The Cahn–Hilliard equation is a fundamental evolution equation for conserved order parameters, commonly used to model phase separation, spinodal decomposition, and coarsening in alloys and porous media [48], [49], [50], [51], [52]. Chemo-elastic phase-field models incorporate both elastic strain energy and mechanical equilibrium, with stress states influencing the chemical potential and diffusion [53], [54]. These models have been employed to study the void swelling phenomenon, precipitate coarsening, and changes in precipitate morphology as a function of applied stresses, and it has been established that the observed growth paths and coarsening exponents can be influenced by the elastic interactions [[55], [56], [57], [58], [59], [60]]. However, the use of these methods to model the behavior of ensembles of helium bubbles in iron under residual equibiaxial stress conditions remains limited.
Existing computational work on the FeHe has mostly focused on the migration of a single bubble under various thermal gradients or simplified stress conditions, which has been insufficient to investigate the coarsening of multiple bubbles under realistic residual stresses [[61], [62]]. Experiments on stress-influenced coarsening in porous solids and precipitate systems reveal significant enhancements or reductions in the coarsening rate due to elastic fields, but most studies are conducted under idealized geometries and do not account for stress symmetry in realistic multi-bubble ensembles [[63], [64], [65]]. A theoretical model of defect diffusion under pressure indicates that defect mobility should change with pressure via the activation volume, implying that diffusivity should decrease with compression and increase with tension [[61], [66], [67], [68]]. However, such physics is not often incorporated in phase-field simulations of helium bubbles in iron, and is rarely employed to calculate stress-dependent coarsening rates for temperature conditions found in reactors [[69], [70]]. Furthermore, the effect of equibiaxial compression compared to equibiaxial tension on the metrics of multi-bubble Ostwald ripening, such as bubble number density, average radius, Arrhenius trends, and LSW scaling, has not been systematically evaluated under controlled conditions. The gaps stimulate a comprehensive chemo-elastic phase field study that explicitly incorporates the effects of stress, mobility dependence on temperature, and elastic interactions in multi-bubble coarsening [[71], [72]].
This work quantifies the combined effect of temperature and residual stress on He bubble coarsening in Fe using a chemo-elastic phase-field model. A Cahn–Hilliard equation was solved for a conserved order parameter, which represents the bubble phase, the chemical driving force was coupled into the anisotropic elasticity in a Fourier-spectral formulation [[73], [74], [75]]. This work has three contributions. First, the stress-dependent mobility law provides the physical explanation for why the coarsening rate at a fixed time is different under compressive and tensile stress. Second, the coarsening kinetics are evaluated using normalized-time comparisons and finite-window fits, and the recovered apparent activation energy is consistent with the 0.20-eV activation energy prescribed in the mobility law. The model is based on a symmetric Ginzburg–Landau potential for the chemical free energy and incorporates a stress-dependent mobility term that represents activation-volume-controlled diffusion [[23], [76], [77]]. We focus stress reactor relevant conditions from 800 to 1000 K and compare three stress states: no stress, equibiaxial compression, and tensile stress. We extract quantitative kinetics of the late-stage coarsening, including the bubble number density, average radius, as well as Arrhenius behavior, to understand how stress symmetry changes the ripening kinetics. By this method, a mechanistic understanding of the evolution of He bubbles under stress in irradiated steels is obtained, and quantitative benchmarks for future experiments and modeling are given.

2. Model and methods

2.1. Phase-field model

Helium-bubble coarsening in α‑iron under a residual biaxial stress is described by a conserved phase-field (Cahn–Hilliard) model with stress-dependent kinetics [78]. The microstructure is represented by a single conserved parameter 𝜂⁡(𝐫,𝑡) with 𝜂 =1 inside a He bubble and 𝜂 =0 in the Fe matrix, the two phases being joined by a diffuse interface [56]. All thermodynamic, elastic, and kinetic terms are expressed as a function of this single field, such that the entire model remains directly connected to 𝜂 and to its governing phase-field equation [[57], [61]].
The evolution of η is governed by the Cahn–Hilliard Eq. [[79], [80], [81], [82]].(1)𝜕𝜂𝜕𝑡=∇·[𝑀⁡(𝑇,𝜎)∇𝜇]
Where 𝑀⁡(𝑇,𝜎) the mobility in Eq. (16) and μ is the chemical potential Eq. (5). Since residual stress is spatially uniform and the mobility depends only on temperature and the applied stress, 𝑀⁡(𝑇,𝜎) is constant in space. Therefore, Eq. (1) is the governing phase field equation where free energy defines μ, and mobility defines the kinetics.

2.1.1. Free energy

The total free energy is written as the spatial integral of chemical, gradient, and elastic contributions,(2)𝐹=∫Ω[𝑓ch⁡(𝜂)+𝜅2⁢|∇𝜂|2+𝑓el⁡(𝜂)]dΩ
Here 𝑓ch is the local chemical free-energy density, κ is the gradient-energy coefficient where the gradient term penalizes diffuse, and 𝑓el is the elastic strain-energy density (Section 2.2.2) [[46], [80], [83], [84]].
The local chemical free energy is described by a symmetric Ginzburg–Landau double-well potential [85].(3)𝑓ch⁡(𝜂)=𝐴𝜂2⁢(1−𝜂)2with minima at 𝜂 =0 and 𝜂 =1. The chemical driving force is(4)𝜇ch=𝜕𝑓ch𝜕𝜂=2⁢𝐴𝜂⁢(1−𝜂)⁢(1−2⁢𝜂)
In all simulations, A = 1.2 and κ = 4.2 (dimensionless). Here, A controls the height of the barrier between the two minima, while κ controls the gradient energy contribution and hence the diffuse-interface width. Eq. (4) is the first term that will appear inside μ.

2.1.2. Chemical potential

Taking the variational derivative of Eq. (2) with respect to 𝜂 gives the generalized chemical potential [[56], [86]].(5)𝜇=𝛿𝐹𝛿𝜂=𝜇ch−𝜅∇2𝜂+𝜇eland, inserting the double well of Eq. (4),(6)𝜇=2⁢𝐴𝜂(1−𝜂)⁢(1−2⁢𝜂)−𝜅∇2𝜂+𝜇el
The first term promotes phase separation, the second term penalizes curvature and interfacial roughness, and the third term 𝜇el, is the elastic driving force arising from the interaction of the residual stress field with the evolving bubble morphology defined in Eq. (15) [[61], [79]].

2.2. Elastic coupling

2.2.1. Eigen strain

Elastic interactions are incorporated through a composition-dependent eigenstrain field following the standard micro-elasticity approach for phase-field model [87]. The eigenstrain tensor is interpolated between the matrix and bubble phases using the interpolation function h (η) = 𝜂𝑝, where the exponent 𝑝 controls the transition width. The Eigen strain is expressed as(7)𝜀∗𝑖𝑗=𝜀0𝑖𝑗⁢ℎ⁡(𝜂)
With 𝜀0𝑖𝑗 the stress-free transformation strain. The derivative of the interpolation function, which appears in the variational derivative of the free energy,(8)𝜕ℎ𝜕𝜂=𝑝𝜂(𝑝−1)
For the current simulations, a quadratic interpolation is employed with 𝑝 = 2. The eigenstrain is taken as purely dilatational, 𝜀∗𝑥𝑥 =𝜀∗𝑦𝑦 =𝜀0⁢ℎ⁡(𝜂), with 𝜀0 =0.005 and 𝜀∗𝑥𝑦= 0. Thus, no eigenstrain anisotropy is imposed. The eigenstrain represents a prescribed bubble–matrix misfit and contributes to the elastic chemical potential during the phase-field evolution. At mechanical equilibrium, the elastic free energy does not change with small displacements. Its contribution to the phase-field driving force therefore comes only through how the eignstrain changes with the order parameter. This gives the elastic chemical potential 𝜇el =𝜕𝑓el𝜕𝜂 = −𝜎𝑖𝑗⁢𝜕𝜀∗𝑖𝑗/𝜕𝜂 where 𝜕𝜀∗𝑖𝑗/𝜕𝜂 =𝜀0𝑖𝑗⁢d⁢ℎ⁡/d⁢𝜂 and d⁢ℎ⁡/d⁢𝜂 = 𝑝𝜂(𝑝−1). This term is calculated through the total stress field so, the applied stress is incorporated directly into the driving force through the elastic stress term rather than only through mobility [57]. The derivative ℎ′⁡(𝜂) is what couples the elastic energy back into 𝜇el (Eq. 13).

2.2.2. Strain, and elastic energy

Under small-strain kinematics, the total strain field 𝜀𝑖𝑗 is obtained from the displacement vector u = (𝑢𝑥, 𝑢𝑦).(9)𝜀𝑖𝑗=12(𝜕𝑢𝑖𝜕𝑥𝑗+𝜕𝑢𝑗𝜕𝑥𝑖)
Which in two dimensions gives 𝜀𝑥𝑥 =𝜕𝑢𝑥𝜕𝑥, 𝜀𝑦𝑦 =𝜕𝑢𝑦𝜕𝑦, and 𝜀𝑥𝑦 =12 (𝜕𝑢𝑥𝜕𝑦+𝜕𝑢𝑦𝜕𝑥).
The elastic strain 𝜀el𝑖𝑗 is then defined by subtracting the Eigen strain contribution 𝜀∗𝑖𝑗 from the total strain [46].(10)𝜀el𝑖𝑗=𝜀𝑖𝑗−𝜀∗𝑖𝑗⁡(𝜂)
And the stress follows the cubic-anisotropic constitutive law(11)σ𝑖𝑗=𝐶𝑖𝑗𝑘𝑙⁢𝜀el𝑘𝑙
The elastic constants for α‑iron at room temperature are [88] 𝐶11 = 180 GPa, 𝐶12 = 122 GPa,𝐶44 = 104 GPa. In solver units these map to 𝐶11 = 2.33, so that one model stress unit corresponds to 180/2.33 ≈ 77.2 GPa.
The elastic strain-energy density is calculated from [89].(12)𝑓el=12σ𝑖𝑗⁢𝜀el𝑖𝑗
The elastic driving force is derived by taking the variation of 𝑓el with respect to the η, which yields(13)𝜇el=𝜕𝑓el𝜕𝜂=−σ𝑖𝑗⁢𝜀0𝑖𝑗⁢ℎ′⁡(𝜂)
The eigenstrain field is defined as 𝜀∗𝑖𝑗= 𝜀0𝑖𝑗⁢ℎ⁡(𝜂) making its derivative 𝜕𝜀∗𝑖𝑗𝜕𝜂 = 𝜀0𝑖𝑗⁢𝑑ℎ𝑑𝜂. This approach follows the phase-field microelasticity theory [90] where the elastic energy is expressed as a functional of the phase field and the total free energy is minimized with respect to the displacement field. Eq. (13) is 𝜇el the one that appears in Eqs. (5), (6) and represents the point at which the elastic sub-model is reconnected to the main Cahn-Hilliard equation.
To evaluate Eq. (13) the stress field must be known. At every Cahn–Hilliard time step, the elastic field is obtained by enforcing mechanical equilibrium(14)𝜕σ𝑖𝑗𝜕𝑥𝑗=0
This is solved in Fourier space using the wave vector 𝑘 = (𝑘𝑥, 𝑘𝑦). Following the standard microelasticity approach [[91], [92], [93]], Eigen stress transformed into Fourier space, and displacement field is then obtained from the Fourier-space linear system, and the strain field is recovered by inverse transformation. The Eigen strain-induced stress field is first evaluated in Fourier space.

2.3. Temperature and stress dependent mobility

The mobility entering Eq. (1) is formulated in two separated stages. First, the stress free baseline follows Arrhenius law referenced to 𝑇ref = 900 K,(15)𝑀⁡(𝑇)=𝑀0⁡exp⁡[−(𝑄𝑘𝐵)⁢(1𝑇−1𝑇ref)]
This follows the standard Arrhenius law of helium diffusion in BCC Fe, as derived from atomistic simulations and widely used in phase-field models of He bubble evolution [[61], [94]].
Second, stress-assisted diffusion is incorporated through a pressure-dependent exponential factor, such that the case-dependent mobility becomes(16)𝑀⁡(𝑇,𝜎)=𝑀⁡(𝑇)⁢exp⁡(−𝑝∆𝑉∗𝑘𝐵⁢𝑇)where𝑝=−𝜎ℎ
This form is obtained from the thermodynamic definition of the activation volume. For an isotropic activation process, the migration barrier responds only to the hydrostatic component of stress, expressed as the mechanical pressure 𝑝 =−𝜎ℎ. This pressure shifts the activation Gibbs energy by ∆𝐺∗ =𝑝 ∆𝑉∗ where ∆𝑉∗ is the activation volume. The mobility therefore develops a stress-dependent factor exp⁡[(−𝑝∆𝑉∗𝑘𝐵⁢𝑇)], where 𝑝 is mechanical pressure derived from the applied residual stress, not the internal gas pressure of the bubble. In the present implementation, 𝑀0 = 1.0, Q = 0.20, and 𝑘𝐵 = 8.6 × 10−5 eV K−1, The activation volume is taken as ∆𝑉∗ =0.0037 nm3[16] with applied biaxial stress 𝜎biax =±2 GPa. In solver units, 1 model stress unit corresponds to 77.2 GPa [61]. 𝑀⁡(𝑇,𝜎) Eq. (16) is the mobility which is used consistently in the governing equation in Eq. (1) and in the numerical update Eq. (17). 𝑀⁡(𝑇) It only represents the no stress case, and does not appear independently in the kinetic formulation.

2.4. Numerical solution

The governing Cahn-Hilliard equation Eq. (1) with chemical potential of Eq. (6) and elastic equations are solved on a periodic square domain of size N × N with N = 512. The dimensionless grid spacing is chosen as Δ𝑥∗ = Δ𝑦∗ = 1.0, and the time step is Δ𝑡∗= 0.015. All following lengths are dimensionless.
Because the mobility 𝑀⁡(𝑇,𝜎) is spatially constant, Eq. (1) is linear in its highest-order term and is integrated with a semi-implicit Fourier-spectral scheme [[95], [96]], the nonlinear chemical and elastic contributions are treated explicitly, while the stabilizing gradient term is treated implicitly. The numerical solution in Fourier space is given by(17)̂𝜂𝑛+1=̂𝜂𝑛−Δ⁢𝑡⁢𝑀⁡(𝑇,𝜎)⁢𝑘2⁢Ƒ⁢{𝜇𝑛ch+𝜇𝑛el}1+∆𝑡𝑀⁡(𝑇,𝜎)⁢𝜅⁢𝑘4
where Ƒ denotes the Fourier transform, 𝑘2 =𝑘2𝑥 +𝑘2𝑦. This semi-implicit treatment is essential for numerical stability and has been extended to incorporate elastic driving forces and variable mobilities [97].

3. Results and discussion

3.1. Temperature effects on bubble coarsening

Fig. 1 shows the microstructural evolution of He bubbles in Fe at 800 K, 900 K, and 1000 K. Figs.1 (a) – (c) show the microstructural evolution at 800−1000 K, where initially random nucleated small He bubbles are formed. Figs.1 (d) – (f) show the coarsened morphologies of He bubbles at 𝑡∗ =450 for the three temperatures, it can be seen that the coarsening is temperature-dependent, and the number of bubbles becomes smaller, and their size is larger at 1000 K than at 800 K. This accelerated coarsening is in agreement with the Arrhenius behavior of diffusion mobility shown in Eq. (15) [61].
The elastic driving force is not negligible in the present simulation. The RMS ratio 𝜇el/𝜇chem increases from 4.6% at 𝑡 =75 to 11.5% at 𝑡 =1800. Its maximum observed value is 10.6%. This happens because bubbles grow larger over time. Elastic energy depends on bubble size, but chemical and gradient energies depend on the phase interface. As bubbles grow during coarsening, the elastic contribution therefore becomes more important. The elastic constants of the bubble phase are considered equal to the matrix (Voigt – Taylor scheme), which indicates that if the shear moduli are equal, then the bubble shape does not change under applied stress [[63], [91]].
The interfacial energy is isotropic, which does not favor any direction [[79], [80]]. In addition, the applied residual stress is biaxial and uniform and Eigen strain is small but non zero, and moduli is also homogeneous, that is why hydrostatic stress𝜎ℎ =13⁢(𝜎𝑥𝑥+𝜎𝑦𝑦+𝜎𝑧𝑧), and the corresponding mechanical pressure is 𝑝 =−𝜎ℎ are spatially uniform and do not derive anisotropic diffusion [[61], [66]]. Therefore, no morphological change is expected, as applied stress effects coarsening through activation volume dependence of mobility.
Fig. 2 quantitatively calculates the evolution of He bubbles and interface compactness, which is defined as the total perimeter to the total bubble area from 800 to 1000 K. The microstructural evolution presents four stages: initial coalescence stage (0 ≤𝑡∗ ≤250), growth stage (250 ≤𝑡∗ ≤800), diffusion-controlled Ostwald ripening stage (800 ≤𝑡∗ ≤1400), and late-stage Ostwald ripening stage (1400 ≤𝑡∗ ≤1800). It is found that the number of bubbles decreases rapidly in the initial coalescence stage, indicating that the rate of coalescence is high at 𝑡∗ <250. In this stage, the number of bubbles decreases Δ⁢𝑁/𝑁𝑜 = 14.3%, 28.0%, and 37.0% at 800 K, 900 K, and 1000 K respectively.
The interface compactness is defined as 𝐶⁡(𝑡) =𝑃tot⁡(𝑡)/𝐴tot⁡(𝑡), and 𝐶⁡(𝑡) decreases from 0.336 at 𝑡∗ = 0 to 0.186, 0.172, and 0.161 at 𝑡∗= 250 for 800 K, 900 K, and 1000 K respectively, and this compactness reduction of ∆𝐶 = 0.150, 0.164, and 0.175 indicates the initial coalescence stage. These reductions in bubbles exhibit early-stage bubble coalescence, which leads towards irregular morphology, which then evolves by Ostwald ripening to form well-separated bubbles. In the third stage (800 ≤𝑡∗ ≤1400), the evolution changes to diffusion-controlled Ostwald ripening. Mass is conserved throughout the coarsening, which indicates that the structure evolution is not due to any numerical loss of mass as reported by [76], but rather due to minimization of the interfacial energy.
The quantitative microstructural evolutions for temperatures 800–1000 K are shown in Fig. 3. The increase in temperature causes an increase in 𝑟eff and a decrease in 𝑁bf, as seen in Figs. 3(a) – (b). Therefore, 𝑟eff at t* = 1800 is 18.17, 20.52, and 21.80 for 800–1000 K, respectively, which gives a net increase of ∆𝑟eff = 3.63. At the same time, 𝑁bf decreases from 110 at 800 K to 96 at 900 K and 82 at 1000 K, which gives a net decrease of ∆𝑁bf = 28. In Fig. 3(c), the mean coarsening rate 𝛤c is defined as the average bubble number loss rate 𝛤c =𝑁b⁢0 −𝑁bf/𝑡∗, and it quantifies how fast bubbles are eliminated, it increases from 0.105 at 800 K to 0.121 at 1000 K. The increase of ∆𝛤c = 0.016 is consistent with the Arrhenius dependence of atomic mobility, which indicates that late-stage coarsening is diffusion controlled.
Finally, in Fig. 3(d), it is observed that the overall coalescence efficiency 𝜑c rises from 63.3% at 800 K to 68.0% at 900 K and 72.7% at 1000 K, which is in good agreement with classical kinetic theories of precipitate coarsening [[98], [99]]. The results presented here indicate that the growth and dissolution of bubbles are thermally activated and diffusion-controlled, as the mobility 𝑀⁡(𝑇) obeys the Arrhenius relation given in Eq. (15) with the value of 𝑄 =0.20 eV, which validates that our phase field model shows similar behavior as reported in (Wen et al., 2022) [61].
To investigate the kinetics behavior of He bubbles in Fe, the diffusion-controlled Ostwald ripening stage (800 ≤𝑡∗ ≤1400) is quantitatively analyzed in Fig. 4. In Fig. 4(a), the coarsening coefficient 𝐾 for tetemperatures00–1000 K are 2.99, 4.28, and 5.52 with coefficient of determination R2 = 0.9978, 0.9988, and 0.9993 respectively. These values were obtained by fitting 𝑟3eff =𝐾⁢𝑡∗ +𝑏over the interval 800 ≤𝑡∗ ≤1400. Within the present two-dimensional model, 𝐾 is used as a comparative measure of the coarsening rate. Fig. 4(b) shows measured growth exponents for temperatures 800–1000 K, 𝑛 = 0.287, 0.305, and 0.312, respectively, close to the theoretical value 𝑛 =1/3. The coarsening rate constant follows(18)ln⁡𝐾=ln⁡𝐴0−𝐸𝑎+𝑝∆𝑉∗𝑘𝐵⁢𝑇where 𝐸𝑎 is the activation energy and 𝑝 ∆𝑉∗ represents the effect of stress through activation volume∆𝑉∗.
The coarsening rate constants extracted at the late stage were plotted in an Arrhenius plot, lnK versus 1/T, as shown in Fig. 4(c), and showed a linear relationship, with a slope m = − 2.46 × 10-3 and an activation energy Ea of 0.215 eV. This activation energy 𝐸𝑎 confirms that coarsening kinetics remain thermally activated. Fig. 4(d) shows the relationship between the bubble number and the effective radius for the no-stress cases. For the present two-dimensional simulations, the data are fitted using the relation 𝑁𝑏 ∝r−2eff , which shows linearity, over the selected Stage-3 interval, with R2 ranging from 0.9887 to 0.9903 for all temperatures [[100], [101]].

3.2. Bubble coarsening under compressive stress

The bubble morphologies under residual equi-biaxial compressive stress 𝜎biax= − 2 GPa are shown in Fig. 5. Temporal evolution at 800–1000 K in Figs. 5 (a) – (c) reveals a bubble distribution initially, then it coarsens to larger domains. At 𝑡∗ = 450 in Figs. 5(d) – (f), the density of bubbles is higher, especially at lower temperature, and at 𝑡∗ = 1800, in Figs. 5(g) – (i), there are still more small bubbles as compared with the no stress evolution shown in Fig. 1, which shows slower microstructural coarsening than the no stress case [61]. Overall, temperature is the major accelerating factor, and the rate is modulated by compression.
The quantitative analysis of coarsening under compressive stress 𝜎biax = − 2 GPa are summarized in Fig. 6. It is found that the bubble number 𝑁bf decreases with temperature to 𝑁bf = 146, 127, and 107 for temperature 800–1000 K respectively in Fig. 6(a), but remain higher than the no stressed case, 𝑁bf = 110 at 800 K to 96 at 900 K and 82 at 1000 K, this show slower coarsening under compression. In Fig. 6(b), 𝑟eff is smaller as 𝑟eff = 14.87, 17.16, and 18.42 at t* = 1800 compared with 18.17, 20.52, and 21.80 for temperature 800–1000 K under no stress, respectively. In Fig. 6(c), the fitted growth rate n are in the range of 𝑛 =0.25 −0.29, with R2 = 0.9889, 0.9989, and 0.9928 respectively. For the no stress case the exponent is close to 1/3, consistent with bulk diffusion-limited coarsening. The slightly lower exponent suggests that the coarsening kinetics are slowed down.
The Arrhenius plot of ln 𝐾 versus 1/𝑇 for the coarsening is thermo-activated even in the presence of a compressive stress, as shown in Fig. 6(d). The values of coarsening rate constant 𝐾 are calculated from ∆𝑟3eff versus time for temperature 800–1000 K, their values are 1.55, 2.25, and 3.09, respectively, these values are 44–48% lower than 2.99, 4.28, and 5.52 of no stress case shown in Fig. 4(a), this clearly indicate that compressive stress slows down the Ostwald ripening.
The decrease in the coarsening rate constant 𝐾 is due to the stress-modified mobility factor exp⁡[(−𝑝∆𝑉∗𝑘𝐵⁢𝑇)] (Eq. (16)) where compressive pressure (𝑝 >0) lowers the diffusivity (Wen et al., 2022) [61]. These results are also consistent with activation volume theory for pressure dependent diffusion [[61], [66]] as well as the experimental findings that coarsening in alloy is slowed by compressive stress [[102], [103], [104]].

3.3. Bubble coarsening under tensile stress

Evolutions of He bubbles under residual equi-biaxial tensile stress is shown in Fig.7. Figs. 7(a) – (c) reveal a bubble distribution initially, and Figs. 7(d) – (f) show the morphology at 𝑡∗ = 450 where bubbles are denser as compared to the final time 𝑡∗ = 1800. Bubbles become larger and fewer at higher temperature at 𝑡∗ = 1800, which shows that temperature induces large mobility 𝑀⁡(𝑇) in Eq. (17) [94], as seen in Figs. 7(g) – (i).
When compared to the compressive stress in Fig. 5, the tensile case shows more advanced coarsening at the same times, suggesting that tensile stress, rather than suppressing diffusion kinetics, helps to enhance them. This is expected because tensile stress reduces the pressure term in the stress-assisted mobility factor shown in Eq. (16) and increases the average diffusivity [[61], [66]]. These results are supported by activation volume theory of pressure-dependent diffusion [105].
Fig. 8 summarizes the tensile-stress kinetics. Fig. 8(a) shows a monotonic decrease in bubble number with temperature, but the values are lower than both the no-stress and compressive cases, indicating faster coarsening under tensile stress. It is found that bubble numbers 𝑁bf = 81, 69, and 61 for temperature 800–1000 K remains lower in tensile stress than that of no stressed case, 𝑁bf = 110 at 800 K to 96 at 900 K and 82 at 1000 K, and compressive stress with 𝑁bf = 146, 127, and 107 for temperature 800–1000 K. It clearly shows that tensile stress faster the coarsening rate constant.
In Fig. 8(b), 𝑟eff is consistently larger as 𝑟eff = 22.34, 24.70, and 25.93 compared with 18.17, 20.52, and 21.80 under no stress and compressive stress 𝑟eff = 14.87, 17.16, and 18.42 for temperatures 800–1000 K. In Fig. 8(c), the fitted growth rate n is in the range of 𝑛 =0.310 −0.318, with 𝑅2 = 0.9927 − 0.9988. All values of growth exponents are closer to 1/3 with slight deviation, and the determination coefficient shows an excellent linear fit and is consistent with diffusion-controlled Ostwald ripening [[54], [61], [106]].
In Fig. 8(c), the coarsening rate constant 𝐾 are calculated from ∆𝑟3eff versus time for temperatures 800–1000 K, 𝐾 = 6.01, 7.74, and 9.36 are higher than no stress (2.99, 4.28, and 5.52) and compressive stress (1.55, 2.25, and 3.09), which clearly indicate that tensile stress accelerates coarsening. These values are 70−104% more than no stress and 201−292% than compressive values. The increase in the coarsening rate constant 𝐾 is due to the stress-modified mobility factor exp⁡[(–𝑝∆𝑉∗𝑘𝐵⁢𝑇)] (Eq. (16)), where mechanical pressure (𝑝 <0) enhances the diffusivity (Wen et al., 2022) [61].
Fig. 8(d) maintains a linear Arrhenius relation for ln⁡𝐾 versus 1/T, confirming that coarsening remains thermally activated. Tension promotes coarsening, while compression slows it down, which is completely consistent with the stress sensitive diffusion work previously proposed by Wen et al. [61] and with the recent experimental observations carried out in alloy systems of the same type. The values of the activation volume and diffusion coefficient are also found to be satisfactory as compared with the theoretical values of Fe [[102], [103], [104]].

As shown in Table 1, compressive stress increases the final bubble numbers and decreases both the average bubble radius and the coarsening rate constant 𝐾 relative to no stress, while tensile stress decreases the bubble density and enhances coarsening. These trends are due to pressure dependent mobility 𝑀⁡(𝑇,𝜎).
To determine whether the applied stress changes the coarsening process or changes its rate, we compared the 900 K results using the normalized time 𝜏 =[𝑀⁡(𝑇,𝜎)/𝑀ref]⁢𝑡∗, where 𝑀ref is the mobility at 900 K without applied stress. The comparison between the three stress conditions was carried out only over the normalized-time range that is common to all of them 0 ≤𝜏 ≤992.28. After this time normalization, bubble number, the effective radius, and interface compactness follow closely similar trends. For each quantity, the root-mean-square difference from the no stress case remains below 2%. These results show that, for the stress range and parameters considered here, stress mainly changes the rate of coarsening through the prescribed mobility. (see Supplementary material, Table S1)

3.4. Bubble coarsening kinetics under stress

Fig. 9 compares the He bubble coarsening for no stress, compressive stress −2 GPa, and tensile stress 2 GPa. The hierarchy of the bubble numbers 𝑁bf and average radii 𝑟eff is obviously stress-dependent. Under tensile stress, the bubble number is smallest, and the average radius is largest for the fastest coarsening. Under compressive stress, the bubble number is highest, and the average radius is smallest for the slowest coarsening. At 800 K, for the three states as no stress, compression, and tension, the 𝑁bf = 110, 146, and 81; and for 900 K, 𝑁bf = 96, 127, and 69, and at 1000 K 82, 107, and 61. Their corresponding 𝑟eff = 18.17, 14.87, 22.34 at 800 K, 20.52, 17.16, 24.70 at 900 K and 21.80, 18.42, and 25.93 at 1000 K.
Arrhenius plot (ln 𝐾 versus 1/𝑇) is linear for no stress, compression, and tensile stress, as shown in Fig. 9(c), confirming that coarsening kinetics remain thermally activated. The coarsening rate constant follows ln⁡𝐾 =𝑙𝑛⁡𝐴0 −𝐸𝑎+𝑝∆𝑉∗𝑘𝐵⁢𝑇 (Eq. (18)). The pressure is 𝑝 >0 under compression, which increases the activation energy and makes bubble coarsening slower, and under tensile stress 𝑝 <0, which decreases the activation energy and makes coarsening faster. The 𝐸𝑎 is 0.215 eV, and applying stress ±2 GPa induces a change of 0.03−0.06 eV through activation volume∆𝑉∗, as the values of ln⁡𝐾 for tensile stress are 6.01, 7.74, and 9.36, which are higher than 2.99, 4.28, and 5.52 without stress and 1.55, 2.25, and 3.09 of compressive stress, which clearly indicate that tensile stress accelerates coarsening.
These results are consistent with the activation volume relation Eq. (16), where the stress effect is incorporated into the exponential term exp⁡(−𝑝∆𝑉∗/𝑘𝐵⁢𝑇) of the mobility, as shown in Eq. (16), thus the temperature dependence of the diffusion coefficient is not altered [[61], [66]]. This stress-dependent change in the coarsening rate constant without changing the fundamentals of Ostwald ripening is also observed in other phase-field and experimental studies [[60], [100], [107]]. The coarsening kinetics of no stress state is between the two stress states, and serves as a reference to quantify the asymmetric effect of residual stress on coarsening kinetics.
In Fig. 10, R2 ranges from 0.9433 to 0.9893 in compressive and 0.9904 to 0.9929 in tensile residual stress for all temperatures. In this scaling relation, 𝑁b is proportional to 𝑟−2eff at temperatures 800–1000 K, indicating the mean field ripening behavior of the bubbles even under stress. The fitted slopes obtained from linear regression are (2.06±0.09)×104, (2.19±0.06)×104, and (2.46±0.05)×104 for the compressive stress, while tensile slopes are (2.78±0.05)×104, (3.27±0.08)×104, (3.57 ±0.06)×104 for 800−1000 K. These results indicate that under tensile stress, variations of bubble numbers are significantly larger than under compressive stress. Also, the diffusion-controlled Ostwald ripening mechanism is unchanged by the tension or compression stress [[61], [100], [108]]. Tensile stress preserves linear regime for extended range as compared to compression, and these results shows that stress affects the coarsening rate constant 𝐾 by changing the pre exponential mobility factor exp⁡[(–𝑝∆𝑉∗𝑘𝐵⁢𝑇)], without affecting the diffusion controlled process [[56], [61]].
The calculations are two-dimensional and use equi-biaxial loading, so they do not represent a general three-dimensional anisotropic stress state. The reported coarsening exponents are finite-window apparent values, and the conclusion that the global coarsening metrics are mobility-dominated applies to the selected eigenstrain, stress range, and numerical resolution. These limitations do not affect the main finding of the present control calculations. The elastic contribution is small but nonzero, whereas the measured changes in global coarsening metrics are dominated by the stress-dependent mobility.

4. Conclusion

Helium bubble coarsening under residual stress is a key microstructural process that causes degradation in Fe-based alloys, but the effect of residual stress on bubble ripening kinetics is not completely resolved. In this work, a chemo-elastic phase-field framework, which is based on the Cahn–Hilliard equation, the micro-elasticity, stress-modified mobility law with Arrhenius temperature dependence, and an activation volume term, is introduced. Simulations were performed at temperatures of 800–1000 K, ±2  GPa compressive and tensile stress states, the bubble number density, average radius, and coarsening rate constant 𝐾 were quantified. The coarsening rate constant increases with temperature for the thermally activated diffusion mechanism. Compressive residual stress slows down the coarsening rate constant, leading to higher bubble numbers and smaller average size. A tensile residual stress accelerates coarsening and results in fewer bubbles with larger radii. The fitted Stage-3 coarsening-rate parameter 𝐾 follows the same trend. Within the present model, this stress effect is mainly associated with the prescribed pressure-dependent mobility; the elastic contribution is small but nonzero. The quantitative prediction of stress-driven He bubble evolution in Fe-based structural materials provides an integrated theoretical basis for multiple bubble coalescence and helps design radiation-tolerant alloys for nuclear reactor components.
